sections.title: Jackson Park Becomes A Fair
sections.voiceover: For six months in 1893, Jackson Park was not a park. It was a fair. The World's Columbian Exposition was built to mark four hundred years since Columbus reached the Americas. The dedication ceremonies were held in October of 1892, near the four-hundredth anniversary, but the gates did not open to the public until the first of May the next year. The grounds covered about six hundred and eighty-six acres of lakefront that had been mostly marsh and sand. The whole thing cost more than twenty-eight million dollars. And almost none of it was meant to last. On opening day, President Grover Cleveland stood on a platform at the head of the Court of Honor. A little after noon he pressed a golden telegraph key, and the signal started the great steam engine over in Machinery Hall. Flags dropped, fountains rose, and a choir broke into the Hallelujah chorus. About two hundred thousand people were there to see it. The timing was strange. A week after the gates opened, the Panic of 1893 reached Chicago, a financial collapse that became the worst depression the country had seen. Banks failed and factories closed. By that winter, with the fair's work gone, something like a hundred thousand men were out of work on Chicago's streets. The White City sold a dream of order at the exact moment the economy outside it was falling apart.

sections.title: Burnham And Olmsted Build The Set
sections.voiceover: Daniel Burnham, a Chicago architect, was the chief of construction. He oversaw nearly two hundred buildings and the army of workers who raised them. To pick the look of the main halls, he chose ten of the country's leading firms, five from Chicago and five from the East, so the fair would feel national. Richard Morris Hunt of New York drew the Administration Building. Charles McKim's firm did the Agriculture Building. Burnham gave them one shared rule. Their cornices would meet at a single height, sixty feet, and they would all be white. Frederick Law Olmsted, who had laid out New York's Central Park, took the swampy ground and turned it into lagoons and a wooded island. What Olmsted built was a stage. What Burnham built was the set. At the center stood the Court of Honor, a ring of enormous halls finished in white over wood and a fiber called staff. They were not marble. They were plaster and burlap and lath, made to photograph like stone. The largest of them, the Manufactures and Liberal Arts Building, covered nearly thirty-two acres under one roof, the biggest building in the world at the time. Crews worked through a brutal Chicago winter to raise it all on a deadline, and the fair's own medical bureau later counted thirty-two deaths during construction. Almost the only hall that broke the white scheme was Louis Sullivan's Transportation Building, off to one side, with colored walls and a great arched Golden Door. Sullivan thought the rest of it was a mistake. He wrote later that the classical fashion the fair made popular had set American architecture back by half a century. At night the basin was strung with electric light, thousands of bulbs at once, in a decade when most American homes still burned gas or oil. People started calling it the White City.

sections.title: Beauty As An Argument
sections.voiceover: The name stuck, and it meant more than the color of the plaster. The fair was beautiful, and the fair was an argument. It laid the world out as a ladder. Northern Europe and white America stood at the top, in the clean geometry of the Court of Honor. Everyone else was sorted onto the rungs below. And you could walk that argument from one end to the other. West of the Court of Honor ran the Midway Plaisance, a strip about a mile long. Frederic Ward Putnam, a Harvard ethnologist, helped organize it as a kind of living museum of peoples. There were villages up and down it. A German village, an Irish village, a street in Cairo with camels and dancers, a Dahomey village brought from West Africa, an encampment meant to stand for Native American life. The idea built into the layout was that a visitor would pass these displays and read them as stages of human progress, the so-called civilized at one end and the so-called primitive at the other. The closer a group sat to the White City, the more advanced the fair meant to call it. The villages of Africans and Native Americans were placed at the far end. People were recruited for small pay, shipped to Chicago, and put on view for the summer. The science was a costume. What it actually taught was rank. Rising over the whole strip was the Ferris Wheel, the fair's answer to the Eiffel Tower of the Paris exposition four years before. George Washington Gale Ferris Junior, a bridge engineer, designed it. It stood two hundred and sixty-four feet tall, with thirty-six cars that could hold sixty people each, more than two thousand riders at once. A turn on the wheel cost fifty cents, the same as admission to the entire fair. About a million and a half people paid it. The wheel rose above the villages, and the crowd looked down on both.

sections.title: Twenty-Seven Million And An Omission
sections.voiceover: About twenty-seven million people came through the gates that season. On a single day in October, called Chicago Day, the fair drew more than seven hundred and fifty thousand, a record for an outdoor event. And while those crowds moved through the White City, a small group of Black Americans set out to tell them what the fair was leaving out. The organizers had refused to give African Americans any real part in planning the exposition. There was no building, no commission, no place at the table. Ida B. Wells, the anti-lynching journalist, had a different plan. A year earlier, her newspaper office in Memphis had been destroyed by a mob after she wrote about the lynching of three Black grocers, and she had been driven out of the South. She came to the fair carrying that story. With Frederick Douglass, the educator Irvine Garland Penn, and the lawyer Ferdinand Barnett, who would later become her husband, she put together a pamphlet. They called it The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition. It came out on the thirtieth of August. It ran through the achievements of Black Americans in the thirty years since slavery had ended. It also laid out the convict-lease system, the laws stripping the vote, and the lynchings spreading across the South, with names and numbers. The fair told a story of progress. The pamphlet told the other half of it.

sections.title: A Desk In The Haitian Building
sections.voiceover: Wells wrote the preface. The exclusion, she wrote, had created, literally and figuratively, a White City, in the building of which the Colored American was allowed no helping hand, and in its glorious success he had no share. They printed the pamphlet in several languages, so foreign visitors could read it. Douglass had a base for the work. He was serving as a commissioner for the Republic of Haiti, and Haiti had its own building at the fair. He gave Wells a desk inside it. Day after day, the two of them handed the pamphlet to passing visitors, many of them from abroad. By the end, ten thousand copies were out, and Wells later said the message had reached far more people than that. There was one day the fair set aside for Black Americans, the twenty-fifth of August. The organizers called it Colored American Day. Wells wanted nothing to do with it. She saw it as a token, and she was furious at reports that officials meant to draw a crowd with free watermelon. She stayed away. Douglass went. He was in his seventies by then, and when he rose to speak, hecklers in the crowd jeered at him about the Negro problem. He set his prepared pages down. He told them there was no Negro problem. The real problem, he said, was whether the American people had loyalty enough, and honor enough, to live up to their own Constitution. The young poet Paul Laurence Dunbar, who was working at the fair as a washroom attendant, read his verse that day. Wells went to hear what people were saying about it, and she came away moved. She later told Douglass that her youth had made her overreact. The day had not been a mockery after all.

sections.title: Hyde Park East And What Stayed
sections.voiceover: The fair changed this lakefront in a way that outlasted the plaster. To carry the crowds out to Jackson Park, the city had the Illinois Central Railroad lift its tracks. The line that ran along the lake was raised up onto a solid embankment, a long wall of earth and stone with the trains running on top. The first ordinance for the work passed in May of 1892, a full year before the gates opened. That wall cut the neighborhood in two. The blocks between the tracks and the lake became a place apart, reached by ducking under the embankment, and people came to call it Hyde Park East. The fair did not end on a high note. Two days before it closed, a man with a grievance shot Mayor Carter Harrison dead in his own home, and the planned closing ceremony was called off. The gates shut for good on the thirtieth of October. The fair had done what almost no American exposition had done before. It closed with cash left over, the first to turn a profit, even in the teeth of the depression outside. The White City itself was already coming down, and much of what was left burned the following summer. But the embankment stayed. The lagoons stayed. Olmsted's wooded island stayed. And the lakefront the fair had made glamorous was now valuable ground. The question of who that ground belonged to, and who would be welcome on it, was just ahead.
